Case study · production agent system

An agent fleet that cannot send anything without me

The work that closes deals — research, qualification, proposals, follow-up timing — was all manual. The CRM I specified and now run my business on has an orchestrator agent — Oreo — over 18 specialists that do that work and queue it. Exactly one module is allowed to send, and only after a human approves the row.

In short

Problem
Pipeline research, qualification, proposals and follow-up timing were manual. An agent allowed to email a customer unsupervised is a liability, not a feature.
My contribution
I own the requirements, the architecture, Oreo's prompt and the 18 specialist prompts, the review, the deployment and the daily operation. AI coding tools wrote most of the implementation. When it is wrong in production, it is mine to fix.
Evidence
The approval path below is drawn from the running system. The repository is private, so there is no code link — a walkthrough on request.
Status
Daily production use; formal evaluation pending. No test set exists for this fleet, so no accuracy claim is made for it anywhere on this site.

The shape of it

How a request moves through

Every path that reaches a customer ends at the same row in the same table, and that row does nothing until a person clicks approve.

  • GatedEmail, text messages and proposals — anything a customer receives. These queue as a PendingAction row and wait for a person.
  • Not gatedInternal actions: logging an activity, scoring a lead, scheduling a task, writing a briefing. These run without approval, and nothing in that list reaches a customer.

Specialists have no database access of their own and reach data only through Oreo. That keeps credentials and write access in one place and makes every agent run reviewable.

Decisions

Four worth explaining

Two ways to call an agent

run_agent_skill invokes a specialist for one schema-validated output: score this lead, write this proposal. ask_agent opens a persistent thread when the task needs judgment — the specialist replies with a needs list, Oreo fetches that data with its own tools, and the conversation continues. One is a function call; the other is a colleague who can ask a question back.

Knowing what it costs

Per-agent model tiering, cost attribution per run, a daily token budget that short-circuits the fleet, a research cache, exponential-backoff retries, and every run logged to an agent_runs table. Cost is blended on a 3:1 input/output ratio, because averaging the two rates evenly overstates it by roughly 2x.

Vision extraction that replaced a paid service

Merchant processing statements are read straight from PDF by a vision model, with no per-processor parsers. Every figure is either printed on the statement or derived from one by arithmetic. A regex classifier runs independently, and disagreements go to a human instead of being auto-resolved.

Post-call intelligence

A Twilio recording becomes a speaker-separated Deepgram transcript, then a structured review — outcome, sentiment, objections, next steps, coaching tip — written back to the lead's timeline.

Ownership

What I did and what the coding agents did

I own requirements, architecture, agent prompts, review, testing, deployment and operation. AI coding tools — Claude Code, mostly — wrote most of the implementation. The decisions that shaped this system are mine: Oreo-only data access, one sending module, the approval gate, the model tiering, and the rule that a disagreement between the vision extractor and the regex classifier goes to a person rather than being auto-resolved.

I am not claiming to have hand-written 315 endpoints. What I claim is that I can specify a system precisely enough that agents build the right thing, catch it when they don't, and run the result as a business depends on it — because one does.

The honest gap is measurement. This fleet has no evals. The next evaluation project is lead scoring and statement extraction, where being wrong costs money and the right answer is checkable — the same harness as the support assistant.
